To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the prevalence of miosis and aneuploides in cleavage-stage embryos are much higher than the previously reported.

mitotic errors contribute to the abnormality in a significant percentage of good-quality IVF embryos, and the mitotic errors were contributed mainly by endoreduplications, non-disjunction, anaphase lag and chromosomal breakage.

(1) 25% of the studied cleavage embryos are aneuploid; (2) 25% have mosaic aneuploidies; (3) 33.3% are diploid/aneusomy mosaic; (4) 25% are normal; (5) the mitotic errors contribute to the abnormality of cleavage stage embryo.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the chromosomal abnormalities in the embryos produced by IVF.
the prevalence of moseicism in good quality cleavage stage embryos.
the chromosomal abnormalities in the embryos of young women, and the findings are important in improving the quality of IVF embryos.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
8/12 (66.7%) of the studied cleavage stage embryos had chromosomal abnormalities and 4/12 (33.3 %) were chromosomally normal.

2/12 (16.7%, 95% CI, 2.6–40.8%) of the studied top quality cleavage stage embryos were normal, 6/12 (50%, 95%CI, 22.7–77.3%) were mosaic, 2/12 were diploid/ aneuploid with < 38% abnormality and 2/12 had > = 38% abnormality.
8/12 embryos (66.7%) were abnormal, 3/8 (37.5%) had meiotic errors, and 5/8 (62.5%) had mitotic errors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the aneuploidity rate of top-quality IVF embryos is about 25%, and that mitotic errors contribute about 20% to this rate.
50% of the cleavage stage embryos were mosaic and 25% of them were aneuploid.
the aneuploidity rate of cleavage-stage embryos based on a single blastomere is underestimated and the rate is likely higher than the reported 40–60%.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the aneuploidity rate of embryos at the cleavage stages is significantly higher than the rate reported by single blastomere biopsies.

the current practice of biopsying only a small number of blastomeres from a cleavage stage embryo to determine the aneuploidity of that embryo may not be sufficient to accurately determine the chromosomal status.

the current practice of analysing only 1–2 cells from a cleavage stage embryo may not be adequate to determine the true chromosomal status of an embryo, and the use of more blastomeres is needed to accurately assess embryo quality.
